data.title: My friend grosses $300,000 a year with her pet-sitting business. She pays herself $50,000. Should I do the same?
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

'She currently has about 15 sitters, all independent contractors'

"I'm thinking about starting my own pet-sitting business and am trying to understand how businesses like this are valued." (Photo subject is a model.)

Dear Quentin,

I have an acquaintance who started her own pet-sitting business four years ago.

She has a client list of around 300 people. She says she grossed $300,000 last year and netted $90,000. She told me she paid herself $50,000 and, with deductions, was able to get her taxable income down to around $30,000.

She still does a lot of the pet sitting herself, but she's trying to pull back and hire more sitters. She currently has about 15 sitters, all independent contractors, and says she keeps 20%-30% of each client fee.

She believes she could sell the business in a few years for $300,000. That sounds very high to me. My understanding is that small businesses like this are often valued at roughly 2-3 times net income, although I realize there are other factors involved.

I'm thinking about starting my own pet-sitting business and am trying to understand how businesses like this are valued. I'm asking for input specifically on the business valuation and financial aspects. Thank you in advance.

Dog Lover

Related: My golf buddy worked as a financial adviser. Here's how I knew his friendship was fake.

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

Your friend brings a lot of value to the business as the managing director, the founder - and the person who oversees the client list and the network of dog-sitters.

Dear Dog Lover,

Do what a dog does when it approaches dark, unfamiliar territory: Tread carefully.

For small pet-service/dog-sitting businesses, buyers often value the business based on the seller's discretionary earnings (SDE) rather than just the bottom line. At first glance, pet-sitting services have valuations of around 3X average earnings, while broader pet-grooming services have a valuation of 2X earnings to 2.6X earnings.

A $90,000 net income would suggest a valuation of roughly $300,000, more or less in line with the gross sales. But your friend's $50,000 salary could move that valuation higher if it's not already included in the $90,000 net profit. That could have the valuation closer to $400,000, which sounds aggressive.

Your friend brings a lot of value to the business, as the managing director and founder - and the person who oversees the client list and the network of dog-sitters. There are risks that she would have to include in any prospectus, including the economic backdrop and the likelihood that some dog-sitters do what she does, and take a slice of third parties' pet-sitting fees.

A $90,000 net income would suggest a valuation of roughly $300,000.

The obvious advantage of buying a business such as this is the client list and the fact that it's a going concern, but I'd also want to know how long it took her to get where she is today. That could cut both ways: If it took her 10 years, you're paying for that time; if it took her two years, who's to say that you couldn't create the same business model in your area?

Finding reliable dog sitters who treat the animals with care, dignity and respect may not be as easy as it sounds. You also have less control over what happens to these dogs when they are out of your immediate care. There's a lot of trust involved by both the business owner and the clients who are handing over their beloved pets for hours, days and/or weeks.

Median sale prices of dog-boarding businesses have been volatile over the past five years, says BizBuySell.com. "Prices fell in 2022 as interest rates made acquisitions more expensive, rebounding strongly in 2023 to $500,000, then dropped again in 2024. The market surged in 2025, with median sale price reaching $850,000, a 125% increase over the five-year period."

Related: 'They knocked her down and started biting': My mother, 84, was viciously attacked by her neighbor's two dogs. Do we sue?

Evaluating a big risk

A $850,000 valuation does not sound like a one-woman operation with a list of third-party sitters who may or may not be available on any given day. It's far more likely a business with several employees keeping the dog show going. Valuations, sales and income differ dramatically, depending on how the small- or medium-sized business is structured.

Inflation, interest rates and the job market will all influence the fortunes of these kinds of businesses. During the pandemic, millions of people were working from home and did not need to rely on pet-sitting services. Dogs need walks, sure, but they arguably take up less time than a young child when you're trying to work from home.

Before buying a small business, you would require a client list, at least three years of tax returns, monthly revenues and expenses for at least two years so you can see any of that aforementioned volatility and a profit-and-loss statement signed off on by a reputable banking firm. Get a list of assets (computer systems, property, vehicles etc.).

Check bank and credit-card statements to cross-check reported revenue.

Also ask for bank and credit-card statements to cross-check reported revenue against actual deposits. Are they coming from clients? Does the business have any outstanding debt or liens? Any lawsuits against it for mistreating pets? What are the annual insurance costs and what do they cover exactly? Are insurance contracts transferable?

The client list should show tenure, frequency and average spend per client showing how concentrated the revenue is; Is it coming from a handful of clients or a broader base? That will make a difference to the risk you would be taking on. What are the churn and retention rates for clients? Do they stay a few weeks, months or years?

Do your own due diligence by checking out the business's reviews on sites like Yelp, Trustpilot, Google (GOOG) (GOOGL), social media, and dog-sitting sites. On labor and operations, read the employee or contractor list, paying close attention to pay rates, tenure, noncompete clauses, and whether they are classified as W-2 or 1099. Would the staff stay on after a sale?

Being your own boss means having clients whose bark may be as bad as their bite.

data.title: A new bill in Congress would lower the retirement age to 60. See who would qualify.
data.description:
By Jessica Hall

The proposal is 'well-intentioned, but misguided,' one expert says

Among the civilian labor force, 39.1% of workers hold physically demanding jobs, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

A new bill calling for lowering Social Security's full retirement age from 67 to 60 for workers in physically demanding jobs could put additional strain on the trust fund that backs the program and create a two-tiered system for workers, retirement experts said.

The proposal, the "Blue Collar Social Security Fairness Act," introduced on Wednesday by U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens, a Michigan Democrat, would allow workers in physically demanding jobs to get their full retirement benefits at age 60. Full retirement age is currently 67 for people born in 1960 or later.

The earliest an individual can claim Social Security benefits is at age 62, but doing so results in a benefit that is permanently reduced by as much as 30%. To get their full retirement benefits, a worker must wait until age 67, and waiting until age 70 increases benefits by an additional 24%.

The bill aims to cover jobs such as construction, nursing and manufacturing. The Social Security Administration would create the list of qualifying jobs and update it every three years, according to the proposal.

"If we want to honor the dignity of work in this country, we need to lower the retirement age for physical laborers," Stevens said in a statement.

"Michiganders who work with their hands shouldn't have to work until their bodies give out to retire," she wrote on X. "If you put in the work, you deserve the retirement you earned."

The proposal comes as Americans are living longer, with the result that retirement can last decades. It also comes as Social Security itself faces insolvency in just six years, when benefits would be automatically cut by 22% unless Congress moves to strengthen the system, according to the Social Security trustees. Among the suggestions to shore up the program are raising taxes, requiring the wealthy to pay a larger share of their income into Social Security and raising the full retirement age.

By lowering the full retirement age, the bill moves in the opposite direction from the last changes to the program by Congress, which starting in the 1980s gradually raised the full retirement age from 65 to 67.

"The proposed act is misguided on a number of levels," said Lawrence Samuel, a cultural historian and the author of the a book titled "The Rise and Fall of Retirement in the United States: A Social History."

"First, further fragmenting our already divisive society along the lines of social class is not what this country needs at this time. Second, Americans should be trying to spend more years of their lives working rather than fewer, not only for financial reasons but for the psychological and social benefits that a job provides," Samuel said. "And finally, the phrase 'physically demanding' is vague at best. If you happen to be a New Yorker, have you ever tried to get to your office downtown on the 6 train at 8 a.m.?"

Under the proposal, workers would need to have a total of 20 years in physically demanding jobs throughout their careers or to accumulate 15 points over the years worked in such a job. From age 18 to 34, a worker would earn 0.5 points for each year in a qualifying job. From age 35 to 44, the worker would earn one point per year, while from age 45 to 54, they would earn 1.5 points per year. At age 55 and over, they would earn 2 points each year.

According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, jobs are physically demanding when they require sustained exertion such as climbing, heavy lifting, standing or walking. A total of 39.1% of workers in the civilian labor force hold such jobs, the BLS said.

"Protecting blue-collar workers bypasses the high-stress, physically demanding pink- and light-blue-collar jobs," said Teresa Ghilarducci, a professor of economics and policy analysis at the New School in New York City and an expert on retirement. "There are better ways to help people whose bodies and brains can't keep up with the demands of their jobs."

Stevens did not respond to an interview request. It was unclear how the bill would be funded or whether it would advance in Congress.

"Allowing blue-collar workers to claim Social Security at age 60 would be one of many significant increases in benefits we could easily pay for if only the wealthiest Americans paid the same Social Security tax rate on their earnings that the other 94% of Americans do," said Martin O'Malley, who served as commissioner of Social Security under the Biden administration.

Others said the proposal would complicate Social Security and add to the strains on the program.

"This proposal is well-intentioned, but misguided," Nancy Altman, the president of Social Security Works, an advocacy group, told MarketWatch by email. "Social Security is a universal system. Adjusting the retirement age based on people's occupation would undermine the system's design, introduce unnecessary complexity, and drastically increase the cost of administering Social Security."

Workers may move into and out of physically demanding jobs throughout their career, and defining such jobs would be "complicated and inevitably controversial,' Altman said.

"The real problem is that the so-called penalty for claiming Social Security benefits early is too large. Congress should expand benefits, including making them more generous for people who claim at younger ages, and pay for it by requiring the wealthiest Americans to contribute their fair share," she said.

-Jessica Hall

data.title: 'We made a bad, bad decision': I learned the hard way how to manage my aging father's money
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

'When my father died, his trust was the Bible'

"When my father died, his trust was the Bible." (Photo subjects are models.)

Dear Quentin,

As I read this story ("Social Security overpaid my mother, 82, by $20,000. What else is hiding in her finances?"), the similarities to my own life were apparent.

First, I was a 30-year-old asking questions of my parents. That didn't go well. Then, I was a 50-year-old whose mother was gone and whose 83-year-old father was living in Florida and, like the mother in your story, fiercely independent. And now? I am 74, a senior myself, with two children, ages 30 and 35. I have no grandchildren and I am not married.

So here is my story:

When my father died, his trust was the Bible. I knew nothing about how much he had because, frankly, it didn't matter. The trust was the roadmap. We made a bad, bad decision: We decided that my brother and I would be co-trustees, with equal and independent authority. Notwithstanding what happened to me - and to the attorney my father used - here is how I would counsel my friends:

Phase 1: Through articles from AARP and other reputable sources, I would explain the risks of being a senior today. If someone wants to remain independent, they need to continue educating themselves about the changing world we live in as seniors.

Sadly, the $2,000 payment the 82-year-old mother made to her neighbor for clearing her garage is symptomatic of a lapse in judgment about the basic concepts of money, value and reasonableness, compounded by emotion. That emotion overrode thinking about the message she was sending in its entirety to the recipient of that money.

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

Phase 2: There is rarely a case where a daughter should say to her mother, "I don't need to know" or where a mother says to her daughter, "You don't need to know." When is it time to seek legal advice and put processes in place for all contingencies - for example, what happens if you fall and become incapacitated?

Phase 3: Find an online or local senior group that can teach both mom and daughter how to avoid scams and protect digital assets and financial accounts. Local police departments often offer these kinds of seminars, too.

Lastly, I would make it a joint effort, with the daughter acting as a peer who is also learning and in need of education - not as an overseer.

As always, I hope you and yours are well.

Regular Reader, Now in His 70s

Related: My golf buddy worked as a financial adviser. Here's how I knew his friendship was fake.

Check out The Moneyist's private Facebook group, where members help answer life's thorniest money issues. Post your questions, or weigh in on the latest Moneyist columns.

Giving help is often a lot easier than asking for it.

Dear Reader,

You are in a useful position.

You have cared for aging parents, and now you are a parent yourself in your 70s. You have, as you say, seen the risks from both sides. The implication in your letter is that you and your brother had very different views about how to manage your father's life and/or finances. That can create problems even if both parties have the best interests of their parents in mind. It can lead to a power struggle over how much to intervene and, for example, whether a parent should or should not enter nursing-home care.

Phase 1: Absolutely, as a senior, you can approach your life from two perspectives: You can view your independence and financial affairs as a symbol of your ability to navigate the world without any signs of fatigue or cognitive decline. But we all need help at times in our lives, and the biggest takeaway for all readers should be that it applies to whether you're young or old. Parents help young people get a foot on the property ladder, but it's harder to experience what feels like a role reversal. Giving help is often a lot easier than asking for it.

There are things we can all do, young or old. Setting up automatic payments will reduce both the risk of falling behind on bills. Credit cards and valuables should not be left lying around. Two-factor authentication for accessing her bank accounts is another barrier to criminals. Don't leave computer passwords lying around, and they should not be easy to guess. (How many people access their phone with their year of birth, for example?) Estate-planning documents - life-insurance policies to retirement accounts - should be in a secure place.

Related: 'It doesn't seem fair': I'm retired and have plenty of money. Why can't I qualify for a retail credit card?

Phase 2 is tough. Such conversations are not as easy as they sound. First off, you have to trust your adult children or any third party to give someone either a durable or medical power-of-attorney document. It also takes not a small amount of humility and, perhaps most challenging of all, the realization that we are all temporarily abled, for the most part, and will experience a time when we won't have the ability to steer the ship single-handedly. Slowing down, as you point out, comes with risks and, yes, sometimes, costly errors or judgment.

The best way to have "the talk" with an elderly parent is to make sure it's a two-way conversation. Nobody likes to be patronized. Guardian offers a guide to talking to loved ones about these issues. "Less than one-third of families report having had satisfactory conversations around aging and end-of-life planning, and more than two-thirds of those conversations don't happen until there's a critical emergency or health crisis," it says. The conversation may come as a surprise, it says, "give them the time that they need."

Related: 'I was shoveling sidewalks at 8 years old': I'm a 73-year-old boomer dad with two kids. Here's what I teach them about finance

Phase 3 also involves confronting the ugly side of life. It's hard to raise the subject of bad actors and scammers without the elderly parent or grandparent feeling like they are in some way easily manipulated. Again, it's better to approach this from a "we/I' standpoint. "I'm careful about answering my phone, so I let missed calls go to voicemail. My bank will never text me asking me for a code. If someone calls me, claiming to be from my bank, alerting me to an alleged fraudulent transaction, I hang up and call the number on the back of my bank card."

After all, 10% of all people over the age of 65 experience some form of abuse, according to studies cited by a paper published in the Cureus, an online medical journal. "These rates are often higher in long-term-care facilities such as nursing homes, despite government regulations aimed toward addressing this issue," the researchers wrote. Healthcare professionals "are often undertrained and ill-equipped in diagnosing elder abuse." We all need to be vigilant. That means reviewing documents regularly and keeping logins and passwords in a safe place.

There are many groups that can help. Among them are the Federal Trade Commission (1-877-FTC-HELP (382-4357), the National Council on Aging, AARP's Fraud Watch Network Helpline (877-908-3360), the National Elder Fraud Hotline at 833-372-8311, Adult Protective Services and the Eldercare Locator (toll-free at 1-800-677-1116). Report scams to the Internet Crime Complaint Center, a division of the FBI. Finally, there are signs that an elderly relative needs help, including unpaid bills and the involvement of suspicious third parties.

Vigilance and compassion are key.

data.title: These Gen Z-ers are choosing ETFs over sports bets. How younger investors told us they're building wealth.
data.description:
By Genna Contino

How is Gen Z investing their money? Brokerage data and market surveys show approaches ranging from low-cost retirement accounts and ETFs to individual stocks, gold and REITs

Interviews with more than a dozen young investors and data on their holdings show varying approaches, ranging from market-tracking exchange-traded funds and retirement accounts to individual stocks and more speculative wagers.

While some teenagers may mark their 18th birthdays by buying a lottery ticket or getting a first tattoo, Deon Radcliff Jr. had different priorities.

When the Tulane University freshman woke up on his birthday this August, his first order of business as a legal adult was opening a brokerage account and a high-yield savings account.

Radcliff had accumulated about $16,000 in cash from scholarships paid directly to him, in addition to his full ride at Tulane. He set aside $9,000 to immediately start investing in an S&P 500 SPX index fund, AI stocks, gold (GC00) and real-estate investment trusts.

Radcliff is part of a generation entering the financial markets unusually young, with easier access to investing than previous generations but vastly different amounts of money to put to work. Interviews with more than a dozen young investors and data on their holdings show varying approaches, ranging from market-tracking exchange-traded funds and retirement accounts to individual stocks and more speculative wagers. What they share is an effort to build financial security amid high living costs and an uncertain economic future.

Deon Radcliff Jr. receives his high school diploma from Da Vinci Schools in June.

About four years ago, Radcliff said, he asked his parents if they had investments or any assets to leave behind for him and his little sister. "It was always a constant answer of no," he recalled.

Radcliff, who is from South Los Angeles, said these conversations encouraged him to learn more about money and investing.

"My socioeconomic status has a really big impact on how my future could go, whether I want to be a detriment to my community or where I can benefit from the hardships of my community," he said.

As Radcliff embarks on his investing journey, he has a goal of graduating debt-free with $250,000 in assets. "I think that's 100% doable," he noted.

Here's how Gen Z is investing

The picture that emerges from a recent survey is more conventional than Generation Z's reputation for speculative investing might suggest.

Among Charles Schwab's (SCHW) clients classified as Gen Z - people ages 14 to 29 - 65% planned to add money to their investment portfolios in late-summer 2026, with ETFs the most popular investment, according to a recent sentiment report from the brokerage. Online trading platform Robinhood (HOOD) also says its younger clients favor ETFs "as early building blocks of investing, displaying healthy caution as they start their financial journey."

That doesn't mean young investors are avoiding risk-taking. A Betterment survey published earlier this year by the investing app found more than half of Gen Z respondents redirected money intended for traditional investing toward sports betting over the previous year, while roughly a quarter considered betting to be part of their long-term strategy. Some economists and financial commentators have linked that behavior to economic pessimism and rising living costs.

Taken together, the available data resist a simple characterization of younger investors as either overly cautious or speculative.

"Historically, younger people had a little bit more risk tolerance," said James Kostulias, Schwab's head of trading services. "What we're seeing now is they are a little bit more cautious, a little bit more cynical or a little bit more skeptical than some of the older generations."

New American Playbook: New rules for a new generation - and its money

High-school financial-literacy teachers see that proactive mindset firsthand in their classrooms. Chad Mallo, a financial-literacy teacher in Florida who previously worked in banking for 20 years, said his high-school students are eager to avoid the debt and financial missteps they witnessed growing up.

"They are investing earlier, and they are actually more interested in wealth building," Mallo said. "They see the mistakes their parents are making, and they don't want to make that same mistake."

Gen Z lags "behind other generations in retirement-account and individual-stock ownership, likely due to being less affluent overall," said John McKenna, a senior analyst at the asset- and wealth-management research firm Cerulli Associates. "However, individual-stock ownership, as well as crypto, has risen the last few years, as has ownership of mutual funds and ETFs as part of the day-trading boom from the early 2020s."

While saving for retirement - and saving in general - is important for young people, McKenna said Gen Z-ers often face the more immediate concerns of paying off student loans or credit-card debt. They also are saving for short-term goals, such as a vacation or buying their first home.

To see where this generation is stashing its cash, researchers at Cerulli Associates analyzed Federal Reserve data to map out the financial assets of people under 30. But because the survey only interviewed "heads of household," the data skewed toward Gen Z-ers who were already affluent enough to lead a household at a young age.

Looking at a breakdown of their financial assets, this group kept the biggest share (30.6%) in retirement accounts - though this noticeably lagged behind people in their 30s (38.4%) and 40s (42.4%), who had more time to make contributions. Another 15.9% was held in mutual funds and ETFs, and 8% in individual stocks, both of which also trailed other cohorts. Younger households did hold a larger share of their wealth in cash compared to older generations, with 10.2% of their money in savings accounts and 7.5% in checking - compared to just 8.8% and 6.8%, respectively, for heads of households in their 30s.

Another notable outlier in the data was the "other managed assets" category, which accounted for 22.7% of the wealth in young households. For comparison, this category made up less than 5% of the total wealth for households headed by investors between the ages of 30 and 49. While McKenna noted this is primarily attributed to trust funds, it doesn't mean the average Gen Z-er has a trust to call upon. Instead, that wealth is heavily concentrated among a tiny fraction of young people who already have at least $2 million in financial assets.

Zooming into specific sectors, Gen Z was the most bullish on energy stocks and most bearish on real estate this quarter, according to the Schwab report, and their primary concern over the next three months was an AI bubble. Conversely, Schwab's active traders across all generations were more concerned by global macroeconomic issues, inflation and U.S. politics.

Even as Gen Z embraces traditional strategies like diversified stock portfolios, it's difficult to ignore the rise of prediction markets and sports betting, which are blurring the line between gambling and investing.

"When people feel as though they're falling behind, they will do riskier things. They'll try to pick individual stocks instead of sticking with broad ETFs. They will concentrate on a particular sector, maybe a high-growth sector like technology or AI. Or they're even more likely to get into gambling, all in an effort to try to catch up to their peers," said Alexander Smith, a professor at the Worcester Polytechnic Institute who specializes in behavioral economics.

"Low-income populations do a disproportionate amount of lottery gambling - and the current, modern version of that is how sports gambling has just taken off among young people today," he added.

Young investors don't follow a single financial playbook. Even given common economic pressures, the circumstances and the ways that they put their money to work vary widely.

Gen Z investors are not a monolith. Here's how some of them are putting their money to work.

John Taps, a 26-year-old in-house tax accountant, sticks to safe bets: S&P 500 index funds and gold.

The S&P 500 investor

Name: John Taps

Age: 26

Location: New York City

Occupation: In-house tax accountant

Taps said he watched his parents struggle during the 2008 financial crisis, so he plays it safe with his investments. He strictly avoids sports betting and prediction markets, invests primarily through a Roth IRA and a 401(k), and described his investing strategy as basic and conservative. The majority of his Roth IRA contributions - 80% - are invested in S&P 500 index funds, while he keeps 20% in gold as a hedge against the dollar DXY.

"I wanted to make sure I was not going to make any risky investing decisions - where, if something were to happen, myself and my family would still be OK," said Taps, who recently got engaged. It's about "making safe plays during good times for when the bad times come around," he noted.

The Roth IRA investor

Name: Makayla Wilson

Age: 22

Location: Los Angeles

Occupation: Graduate student

Wilson was introduced to the concept of investing during a college-readiness and financial-literacy class she took in high school, where the teacher, Christopher Jackson, helped students open Roth IRAs on their 18th birthday.

Topics like budgeting and investing weren't discussed at home when Wilson was growing up. She said that Jackson sharing his experience navigating his finances as a Black man made the class relatable.

Wilson, who was raised by a single mom, still contributes to her retirement account today and watches her money grow in index funds. She also used what she learned in the class to help her mother set up auto-pay on recurring payments and increase her credit score so that she could qualify for a car loan.

data.title: How to keep profiting from AI while shielding your portfolio against the risk of a slowdown
data.description:
By Philip van Doorn

Jamie Wilhelm and Sunit Gogia of Fort Washington Investment Advisors expect the AI wave to continue, but describe leading indicators of an eventual downturn

The managers of the Touchstone Large Cap Focused Fund expect the AI wave to continue for a long time, but they are also prepared to detect leading indicators of an eventual slowdown.

You might agree with the consensus that the generative AI build-out will last for years. But as an investor, you should watch for the eventual warning signs of a slowdown and consider how to protect your portfolio through an up-and-down cycle.

Jamie Wilhelm and Sunit Gogia of Fort Washington Investment Advisors manage the $3.6 billion Touchstone Large Cap Focused Fund SICWX, which is rated four stars (the second-highest rating) within Morningstar's "Large Blend" category.

During an interview with MarketWatch, Wilhelm and Gogia looked through the AI build-out cycle and explained how investors might eventually see warnings that the growth burst is ending. They provided insight into how they select companies that are likely to weather storms over the long haul.

This cycle is nothing like the late 1990s tech boom

When the stock of the leading hardware maker enabling a technological paradigm shift rises more than fivefold in only three years, the obvious question for investors is whether we are in the middle of a bubble that will soon burst. Over three years through Thursday, Nvidia's (NVDA) stock returned 441% with dividends reinvested. It now has the largest market capitalization for any publicly traded company, at $5.41 trillion.

Nvidia's sales are still growing rapidly, and the company has improved its profitability, with revenue in the latest quarter more than doubling from a year ago.

Nvidia's stock was the third-largest holding of the Touchstone Large Cap Focused Fund, with a 7.2% allocation as of June 30. The largest holding was Alphabet's stock (GOOGL), making up 9.2% of the fund, followed by Microsoft shares (MSFT) at 7.9%. Rounding out the fund's top five holdings were shares of Apple (AAPL), with a 7.1% position, and Amazon (AMZN) at 6.4%.

Wilhelm said the artificial-intelligence build-out is proceeding in a different way from the dot-com boom that began to deflate in 2000. He said there was "a lot of fiber capacity being laid down ahead of demand" in the 1990s. One might have concerns that there won't be enough demand for all the AI services and associated computing capacity being created now. "But what we have seen so far in this AI cycle," which began with the launch of ChatGPT in November 2022, "is that utilization is very high," he said.

"We still don't have enough compute to serve existing demand," Gogia said. He added that, with some political pushback against the construction of data centers, "there are questions of whether or not the capacity can be brought online."

With the high utilization, "you are seeing a continued investment cycle," Wilhelm said, adding that "it is possible for excess capacity at some point, which can lead to a selloff" in the stock market.

When asked about the decline in Nvidia's forward price/earnings valuation to 16.7 from 25.3 at the end of 2025, even as the stock has risen 20% in 2026, Wilhelm said one reason was the increase in interest rates, "which can affect the multiples of the entire market." Gogia said the pushback against data centers might also have placed a drag on Nvidia's P/E multiple.

Wilhelm expects AI to "impact every area through healthcare, maybe in drug discovery, looking at data," to speed up the processes needed to develop medications and treatment techniques.

But the disruption of AI, and even its efficiency improvements, may not benefit all industries. "Banks have very high labor content. If they can get more productive, it remains to be determined if banks can keep profits and let them flow to the bottom line. We think a lot of that will be competed away," Wilhelm said. That comment points to the long-term philosophy he and Gogia follow when selecting companies in which to invest.

Despite concerns over eventual overcapacity, Gogia remained upbeat: "We think this generative AI wave is a multiyear platform shift. Over time, we will consume way more AI compute than we do today, but there will be periods of oversupply along the way."

Warning signs you may eventually see that the AI cycle is at least taking a breather

Wilhelm and Gogia explained what investors might see in advance of a broad decline in stocks that have soared during the AI build-out.

The large semiconductor manufacturers "are high operating-leverage businesses. If supply begins to outstrip demand, the earnings for these companies go down pretty quickly. You need to be careful," Wilhelm said.

Some investors may not realize that only three years ago, memory-chip maker Micron Technology (MU) posted a net loss of $5.8 billion during its fiscal 2023, when its sales declined 49% from the previous fiscal year. Micron is now the ninth-largest holding of the State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust SPY after its stock has gained 279% so far this year.

Wilhelm said there may eventually be signs of overcapacity for AI-related hardware and services. "You would begin to see the rental prices for AI compute come down. You could see inventory of various items build along the supply chain," including chips and servers.

His comment about prices for AI computing power can be tied to a group of pure-play providers of cloud-computing services, known as neoclouds. This group includes CoreWeave (CRWV), whose revenue for the first half of 2026 more than doubled from the first half of 2025, although the company has continued to post operating losses. CoreWeave has been a volatile stock. It was up 21.4% for 2026 when it closed at $90.13 Thursday. But it was down 35% from a closing peak of $137.98 on May 6, according to FactSet.

Related: NeoCloud stocks like CoreWeave are having a moment - and time's running out to cash in

Long-term investments that can weather industry and market downturns

Wilhelm's comment about price competition wiping out some banks' potential benefits from AI-driven efficiency improvement springs from his and Gogia's focus on companies with competitive moats or that operate in industries with high barriers to entry.

"We buy businesses that have cycles to them, but also make sure we buy businesses that have barriers to entry and can sustain those barriers even when the cycle is over," Wilhelm said.

Despite holding stocks of some very familiar names, listed above, Wilhelm said that all companies in the portfolio he manages with Gogia are in industries "with moderate or high barriers to entry."

"The key is the barrier - or the moat - will protect you from bad management," he said. A specific example is Boeing (BA), which is held by the Touchstone Large Cap Focused Fund. For five years through July 30, 2024, the day before Boeing announced that Kelly Ortberg would take over as CEO the following week, the company's stock had fallen 45%, while the S&P 500 SPX had returned 96%.

Boeing is in the midst of a multiyear turnaround effort. Wilhelm said he had decided to buy the stock even before Ortberg took over the company's management.

"People were wondering why we bought Boeing, but that was normal for us," he said, because he saw long-term value in the stock. "They have a true operator running the company for the first time in a long time," although it will be a long road to operational excellence, he said.

"That goes back to the moat," Wilhelm said, referring to the "global duopoly" for large passenger jets that it shares with Airbus (EADSY).

"That moat protected them against a lot of bad stuff," he said. "They had a series of managers who did not do a good job. And now here we are."

data.title: I'm 77, pay rent and live off Social Security, but I help homeless people. Why are so many people going hungry?
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

'I am a retired senior citizen living check-to-check'

"When I get paid once a month, I pay my rent for the month and stock up on food." (Photo subject is a model.)

Dear Quentin,

I am 77 years old. I am a retired senior citizen living check-to-check. I live off Social Security. When I get paid once a month, I pay my rent for the month and stock up on food, so I have a place to sleep and enough to eat. But I always help homeless people I see on the streets with whatever money I have left over, because nobody should have to go without food in this country.

Doesn't California alone have enough food to feed all of America?

Living Off Social Security

Related: 'I don't use cash': I'm 70 and my home is paid off. I live off Social Security, and I use a credit card for all my spending. Is that risky?

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

Food is probably more valuable than time, but both count.

Dear Living,

You give back, even when you have a modest amount to give.

That's quite something, and I appreciate you taking the time to share your story. You are one of millions of retirees (roughly a third) who rely on Social Security, and it's not easy, especially after you pay your rent and buy groceries. Medicaid, for those who qualify, and Medicare help, of course, but living paycheck-to-paycheck requires no small amount of discipline and thrift.

Here's the headline: It's OK for life not to go as planned. It's OK for you not to give away your last dollar. It's OK to be less than perfect. It's OK. Your generosity is admirable, but you also have a right to protect your own financial security. You don't have to give until there's nothing left for yourself, especially if you need that $5 for an unexpected prescription or even food.

For what it's worth, California does not produce enough food to feed the U.S. It produces about a quarter of all the food consumed in the U.S., including more than one third of the country's vegetables and three-quarters of its fruits and nuts, and the Golden State is the country's biggest milk producer, producing nearly 20% of the nation's milk. (Read more here.

It's OK for you not to give away your last dollar.

Having enough food produced nationally isn't the same thing as every individual having enough money or access to food, as you point out. Food needs to be harvested, transported, stored, sold and - last but not least - purchased. Someone can live in a country with an enormous agricultural surplus and still have an empty refrigerator or live in a food desert.

In fact, one in five Black households in America is located in one of these "food deserts," where people don't have access to fresh ingredients, according to the consulting firm McKinsey & Co. Some critics dislike the term, arguing that grocery chains, municipal decisions and lack of government funding contribute to what they call "food apartheid."

Whether it's contributing to charity, stopping to talk to an elderly neighbor or, as you say, giving something - however modest - to a homeless person, every little bit helps. It could be half a sandwich from a cafe, a coffee or simply a kind word. Food is probably more valuable than time, but both count. You are aware of other people's place in the world and their right to dignity.

The high cost of living is a major contributor to homelessness, alongside a myriad of other factors, including job losses, family breakdowns, mental-health and substance-misuse issues, and a lack of community/social support. Many people, when they experience a particularly challenging chapter in their lives, have people they can call. But not everyone does.

Related: 'My total balance should be $20 million': I invested $1.1 million in a crypto platform. Have I lost it all?

Living on $2,000 a month

Nearly 22 out of every 10,000 Americans - 745,652 people - experienced homelessness in January 2025, according to the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), which measures homelessness across the U.S. on a single night each winter. HUD's definition includes sheltered persons living in some kind of temporary housing.

"Unsheltered" people live outdoors, in cars, in abandoned buildings, or in other places deemed unfit for human habitation, HUD says. People staying with friends are considered homeless if they can't stay longer than 14 days, but they are not included in HUD's data. Native Hawaiians and Pacific Islanders had the highest rate of homelessness: 99.9 people per 10,000.

Living on, say, $2,000 a month is technically possible - if you live in a rent-subsidized accommodation or have other resources to pay for that roof over your head. Monthly essentials like utilities, food and transportation can easily eat up $500-$1,000, leaving little cushion for emergencies or home repairs.

A quarter of American retirees still work part-time.

You're not the only senior American living month-to-month. The real median annual income for households headed by someone 65 or older is close to $60,000, and the average older household spends roughly that amount annually. That doesn't leave much wiggle room. Surviving retirement takes both a realistic mindset and the financial means to back it up.

That financial reality may help explain why nearly a quarter of retirees work part-time, supplementing Social Security, 401(k)s, IRAs and any personal investments. Millions of Americans retire with far less than a six-figure savings account, and being single in retirement removes a second income stream that couples can rely on.

The best defense is saving early, diversifying, living below your means, avoiding credit-card debt and building in room for emergencies and mistakes - because most retirement plans don't account for the financial missteps nearly everyone makes at some point, whether it's buy-now-pay-later purchases or risky stock picks. That's easier to see in retrospect.

And perhaps all of this is why your small acts of generosity mean so much to you. We can all be net contributors, but you can't solve homelessness by yourself. You can, however, buy someone half of your sandwich or offer them a cup of coffee. You can stop to talk to someone who may have gone days, even weeks, without being treated like a human being.

Be kind to others, by all means, but don't forget to be kind to yourself.

data.title: Don't Let Rebate Paperwork Cost You Thousands: Townsend Helps Massachusetts Homeowners Get "Townsend Ready" for Winter
data.description:
Don't Let Rebate Paperwork Cost You Thousands: Townsend Helps Massachusetts Homeowners Get "Townsend Ready" for Winter

Don't Let Rebate Paperwork Cost You Thousands: Townsend Helps Massachusetts Homeowners Get "Townsend Ready" for Winter

PR Newswire

DANVERS, Mass., Sept. 26, 2026

Townsend's dedicated rebate specialist manages the entire paperwork process, helping customers access up to $8,500 in Mass Save rebates

DANVERS, Mass., Sept. 26, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- For some Massachusetts homeowners, an aging heating system may not make it through the winter. Nobody wants to replace a furnace or boiler when it's 10 degrees outside, so it's best to plan now, before the winter cold hits. Townsend says this is exactly where it comes in: helping homeowners through the entire process.

Massachusetts currently has some of the most generous home energy rebates it has ever offered. This is great news for homeowners who need a new system and have been putting it off.

Through Mass Save, the state's energy-efficiency program, homeowners can receive substantial rebates for upgrading to a heat pump. Rebates can range from a few hundred dollars to $8,500, depending on qualifications. Mass Save also offers 0% interest financing through its HEAT Loan program, along with free home energy assessments that identify exactly what upgrades make sense for a home.

The Rebate Process Is Intimidating for a Lot of People, but Townsend Makes It Easy

Most homeowners find the paperwork required for a rebate to be overwhelming and complicated. Between eligibility documentation, contractor forms, and an online portal that, frankly, isn't especially user-friendly, many homeowners get halfway through the process, get frustrated, and then give up, missing out on free money.

This is exactly why Townsend created a dedicated rebate team, led by its rebate specialist, Melissa Clark. Melissa manages the entire rebate process for customers from start to finish. She will also help customers secure financing if needed. She gathers documentation, uploads it to the portal, tracks deadlines, and follows up on any missing information so homeowners get every penny of the rebate they're entitled to. Townsend provides hands-on support throughout the entire process, ensuring nothing falls through the cracks and that customers receive the rebate they qualify for.

"Townsend is one of the only companies that will hold the customer's hand through this whole process," says Jimi Letchford, Chief Growth Officer at Townsend. "Most other companies will say, 'submit your paperwork,' and then leave it all to the customer. That means many people are missing out because the process can be complicated. We don't do that; we have Melissa."

Common Myths That Keep People from Applying for Rebates

The first myth is that homeowners have to completely replace their oil or gas furnace to qualify for a rebate. They don't. Homeowners can install a heat pump as a supplement to an existing fossil fuel system and still receive a rebate. The rebate for a supplemental system is typically a smaller tier than the rebate for a whole-home heat pump conversion, but it's still available.

The second common myth customers believe is that a heat pump can't handle a New England winter. That was true of older systems, but it isn't true anymore. Modern heat pumps are built to perform efficiently even on the coldest days.

Advertised rebate amounts can often be misleading. The rebate a homeowner qualifies for may differ depending on the size and type of system installed. Townsend's sales team is trained to walk customers through this process up front, so there are no surprises once the paperwork is submitted.

The Best Time to Start Is Before You Need To

For homeowners considering financing a project, the process should start with a home energy assessment. That assessment audits the entire home and produces a set of recommendations that becomes the roadmap for the project and the homeowner's rebate eligibility. Most often, the general recommendation is a heat pump paired with some weatherization.

Waiting until a system fails in the dead of winter takes away from planning time. Homeowners who start the process well before winter have time to get an assessment, secure financing, and build a clean rebate application with Townsend's assistance.

"Savings Ready is Townsend Ready, because Townsend does the work for its customers."

The equipment, the financing, and the rebates are all available. What gets in the way most often is the paperwork, a problem Townsend has solved for its customers. For more on Townsend's rebate assistance, visit townsendtotalenergy.com/about/rebates.

About Townsend

Founded in 1931, Townsend is a fourth-generation, family-owned and operated company serving residential and commercial customers throughout Massachusetts, New Hampshire, and Maine. The company provides fuel delivery, HVAC installation and service, and electrical services, and is proud to serve customers across New England. For more information, visit www.townsend360.com or call 978-717-0490.

 Danvers, MA 01923
 Phone: 978-717-0490
 Email: marketing@townsendtotalenergy.com

data.title: imogene + willie and Wrangler® Launch Landmark Collaboration Rooted in American Denim Heritage
data.description:
imogene + willie and Wrangler® Launch Landmark Collaboration Rooted in American Denim Heritage

Drawing from Wrangler's iconic archive, the collection is reimagined through imogene + willie's distinctly American approach to craftsmanship and making.

For more than 75 years, Wrangler® has helped define American denim. For imogene + willie, that legacy has been a source of inspiration and admiration since its founding in 2009. Built on a shared reverence for the craft and heritage of American denim, the two brands have partnered on a landmark collection that pairs Wrangler's defining place in denim history with imogene + willie's enduring commitment to domestic manufacturing.

This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260926678904/en/

Wrangler x imogene + willie collection

To bring this collaboration to life, Wrangler opened its historic archives to the imogene + willie team, granting access to original patterns, including the iconic 1964 vintage 10MWZ, along with its coveted supply of Cone Mills White Oak deadstock selvedge denim. Beyond White Oak, the collection also incorporates fabrics developed with Mount Vernon Mills, the last remaining large-scale denim mill in the United States, alongside original labels, pocket flashers, packaging, and visual assets that were thoughtfully reimagined through imogene + willie's distinctive design process.

"This project began with a deep and enduring admiration," says imogene + willie co-founder Carrie Eddmenson. "Wrangler's story has shaped our own. The blue jean they introduced became a blueprint not just for style, but for integrity, craft, and American identity. Made in America has always been a core tenet of who we are, and who Wrangler helped inspire us to become. For them to join us here at home feels more like a ceremony than a collaboration."

The collaboration was an invitation for imogene + willie to step inside one of the richest histories in American denim. Wrangler entrusted imogene + willie with the freedom to explore decades of craftsmanship, design, and tradition. In return, imogene + willie approached the collection with their steadfast desire to put American materials and manufacturing first, with every detail being considered in pursuit of creating something truly special.

"This partnership allowed us to explore our roots through a fresh lens, resulting in pieces that honor the true artistry behind every single stitch," says Joe Broyles, Vice President of Global Collaborations & Chase at Wrangler. "It is a celebration of our shared passion for preserving denim heritage and an homage to the uncompromising quality that has always defined our brand."

"When you bring together Wrangler's remarkable history with a shared commitment to preserving American craftsmanship, you create something that's larger than a single collection," says K.P. McNeill, CEO of imogene + willie. "From the very beginning, we believed this project should honor the people, mills, and makers who continue to keep this craft alive. We hope it reminds people that extraordinary products can still be built through that level of intention and collaboration."

To highlight the depth of the collaboration, the collection will be released in three distinct drops:

Drop 1 (September 26): The launch begins with selvedge denim in Wrangler's vintage 10MWZ model crafted from Cone Mills White Oak deadstock fabric.

Drop 2 (October 24): This release features Wrangler's signature broken twill across jackets, shirts, and jeans developed with Mount Vernon Mills, the last remaining large-scale denim mill in the United States. Plus vintage-inspired graphic tees, sweatshirts, and accessories.

Drop 3 (November 7): The partnership concludes with additional deadstock denim styles in original western cuts, including a rigid western snap.

Starting Sept. 26, customers can shop the first drop of the collection on Wrangler.com, and in-store and online at imogeneandwillie.com. The collection will range in price from $48 to $350.

ABOUT IMOGENE + WILLIE

imogene + willie is a Nashville-based denim and apparel brand founded in 2009 and built on a simple goal: to make garments that transcend simple trends, and to do it all in the United States. What began as a labor of love, making jeans from start to finish in a converted 1950s Nashville gas station, has grown into a small-but-mighty team producing a diverse collection of denim, outerwear, graphic tees, loungewear, and more, all still made domestically today. In addition to their Nashville flagship store, I+W has expanded their operation to include in-house screen printing, a sewing room in Los Angeles, and a second home in Austin, Texas. To learn more, visit imogeneandwillie.com.

ABOUT WRANGLER

Wrangler®, of Kontoor Brands (NYSE: KTB), has been an icon in authentic American style for more than 75 years. With a rich legacy rooted in the Western lifestyle, Wrangler is committed to offering superior quality and timeless design. Its collections for men, women, and children look and feel great, inspiring all those who wear them to be strong and ready for everyday life. Wrangler is available in retail stores worldwide, including flagship stores in Fort Worth and Greensboro, department stores, mass-market retailers, specialty shops, top western outfitters, and online. For more information, visit Wrangler.com.

jackie@imogeneandwillie.com

data.title: University of Phoenix research recognized as Editor's Choice paper by Glacies
data.description:
University of Phoenix research recognized as Editor's Choice paper by Glacies

University of Phoenix research recognized as Editor's Choice paper by Glacies

PR Newswire

PHOENIX, Sept. 26, 2026

Environmental science education study examining storytelling and AI-supported learning receives Editor's Choice distinction

PHOENIX, Sept. 26, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- University of Phoenix announces that the peer-reviewed study, "Harnessing AI, Virtual Landscapes, and Anthropomorphic Imaginaries to Enhance Environmental Science Education at Jökulsárlón Proglacial Lagoon, Iceland," has been recognized as an Editor's Choice paper by Glacies.

Published in February 2026, the study explores how character-driven narratives and human-centered artificial intelligence can support adult learners in understanding complex environmental science concepts. The article was authored by Jacquelyn Kelly, Ph.D., associate dean, College of General Studies; Dianna Gielstra, Ph.D., full-time faculty, Environmental Science Program, College of General Studies; Tomáš J. Oberding, Ph.D., full-time faculty, Environmental Science Program, College of General Studies; Jim Bruno, MBA, associate dean, College of Business and Information Technology; and Stephanie Cosentino, MAEd, senior instructional designer, University of Phoenix.

The recognition highlights research conducted within the University's "Principles of Environmental Science," a course serving non-science majors and adult learners. The study examined the use of character-driven storytelling and AI-generated imagery, developed through a human-centered, faculty-guided design process, to help learners engage with scientific concepts and environmental systems.

"The cryosphere plays a critical role in Earth's environmental systems, yet it is a topic often reserved for advanced scientific study. We wanted to create an accessible entry point into this important science. By bringing together immersive virtual landscapes, narrative storytelling, and human-centered AI, we designed a learning experience that helps adult learners see scientific processes as connected, dynamic, and relevant to the world around them."

Innovative approaches to environmental science education

The study describes how the course uses a storybook-inspired format to introduce environmental science concepts through approachable characters and narratives. Characters such as Nico Nitrogen, Remi Rock and Waverly Water personify scientific processes and cycles, providing adult learners with accessible entry points into complex topics while maintaining alignment with course learning outcomes.

"Recognition by Glacies as an Editor's Choice paper reflects the quality of scholarship being produced by our faculty and academic leaders," said Briana Houlihan, MBA, dean, College of General Studies. "Research such as this demonstrates how innovative instructional approaches can help make complex scientific concepts more engaging and accessible for adult learners while contributing to broader conversations about teaching, learning and technology's role in design."

Researchers reported positive student responses to the instructional approach. According to the study, 87.1% of surveyed students reported enjoying the anthropomorphic narratives, while 82.0% agreed the approach reinforced systems thinking. Qualitative feedback indicated that narrative framing and consistent visuals helped learners visualize relationships among Earth systems and communicate scientific concepts more effectively.

Supporting engagement among adult learners

The authors present the work as a practical model for courses serving non-science majors and working adults. By combining narrative-based learning experiences with carefully guided AI-supported visual development, the approach seeks to make abstract scientific concepts more approachable while supporting learner engagement and understanding.

The Editor's Choice recognition by Glacies acknowledges the study's contribution to ongoing conversations about environmental science education, instructional design and the thoughtful application of artificial intelligence in higher education learning environments.

Access the study

"Harnessing AI, Virtual Landscapes, and Anthropomorphic Imaginaries to Enhance Environmental Science Education at Jökulsárlón Proglacial Lagoon, Iceland" is available online through Glacies at https://doi.org/10.3390/glacies3010003.

About University of Phoenix
University of Phoenix is Built for Real Life. 50 Years Strong. The University innovates to help working adults enhance their careers and develop skills in a rapidly changing world through flexible online learning, relevant courses, academic AI pillars, and skills-mapped curriculum for associate, bachelor's and master's degree programs. Active students and alumni have access to Career Services for Life® resources including career guidance and tools. For more information, visit phoenix.edu.
